blocks.text: Long ago, an old king of the North fought his last battle. His sword broke in the fighting, and he was badly wounded. That night his young wife found him on the battlefield. "My luck is gone," he told her. "But you will have a son, and he will be a great warrior. Keep the broken pieces of my sword, so that one day they can be made into a new sword for him." The queen escaped from the battle disguised as her own maid, and she was taken to the land of Denmark. There the king of Denmark guessed she was really a queen, because her gold ring always turned cold on her finger just before dawn. So he treated her royally, and soon her son was born. His name was Sigurd.
Sigurd grew up to be a beautiful boy, and very strong. He had a teacher named Regin, who was a wonderful smith and maker of swords.

One day the king told Sigurd to choose a horse for himself. In the woods Sigurd met an old man with a white beard. "Drive all the horses into the river," said the old man, "and choose the one that swims across." Only one horse swam across. His name was Grani, and he came from the family of Sleipnir, Odin's eight-legged horse. He was the best horse in the world. And people say the old man was really Odin himself.
Then Regin came to Sigurd. "There is a great treasure of gold not far from here," he said. "You should win it."
"I've heard of that treasure," said Sigurd. "The dragon Fafnir guards it, and he is so huge and wicked that no one dares to go near him."

Then Regin told Sigurd a story. Fafnir, the dragon, was Regin's own brother. Long ago there had been three brothers: Fafnir, Otter, who could turn himself into an otter whenever he liked, and Regin. One day, Otter was sleeping on a rock by a waterfall in the shape of an otter, when a passing traveler threw a stone and killed him. Their father demanded a payment of gold for his lost son: enough gold to fill Otter's skin and cover it completely.

So the traveler caught a dwarf named Andvari, who had a secret treasure of gold, and took it all, even the dwarf's last little gold ring. The poor dwarf was so angry that he put a curse on the gold. "May this gold bring nothing but bad luck to everyone who owns it," he said.

And the curse came true. Fafnir wanted all the gold for himself. He drove his father and brother away from it, and he turned into a dragon and lay on top of the gold, so that no one could ever take it.
"Make me a good sword," said Sigurd, "and I will fight this dragon."

So Regin made a sword. Sigurd struck it on a lump of iron to test it, and the sword broke. Regin made another, and that one broke too. Then Sigurd went to his mother and asked for the broken pieces of his father's sword. Regin hammered them together into a new sword, so sharp that fire seemed to run along its edges. Its name was Gram. Sigurd struck the lump of iron, and the iron split in two. Then he dropped a tuft of wool into the river and held the sword in the water, and when the wool floated against the blade, it was cut in half. "This sword will do," said Sigurd.

One morning Sigurd and Regin rode out to the heath where the dragon lived. They found the track Fafnir made when he crawled down to a cliff to drink. It was so deep that it looked like a river valley. Sigurd climbed down into that track and dug a pit, and he hid in it with his sword drawn.

Soon the ground began to shake. The dragon was coming! Fafnir came crawling down to the water, snorting and roaring, with a cloud of poison flying in front of him. Sigurd waited until the dragon was right above him. Then he thrust his sword Gram up into the dragon's heart.
The dragon thrashed his tail so hard that rocks broke and trees came crashing down. "Whoever you are," Fafnir hissed, "this gold will be your ruin."
"Everyone dies one day," said Sigurd. "But no brave person lets that stop him from doing what is right." And the dragon lay still. From then on Sigurd was called Fafnir's Bane, the Dragon-Slayer.

Then Regin asked Sigurd to roast the dragon's heart for him to eat. So Sigurd roasted it over a fire. But he touched it to see if it was cooked, and it burned his finger, and he put his finger in his mouth. And as soon as he tasted it, he could understand the language of the birds!
Some birds were chattering in a tree above him.
"There's Sigurd," said one, "roasting the dragon's heart for someone else, when he should eat it himself and become wise."
"There's Regin," said another, "planning to trick Sigurd, who trusts him."
"Sigurd should keep all the gold for himself," said a third.
"And then he should ride over the mountain," said a fourth, "to the place where Brynhild sleeps."

So Sigurd knew that his teacher had been planning to betray him, and with one stroke of his sword he put an end to Regin's treachery. Then he rode to the dragon's cave. Its doors were made of iron, and inside it was full of gold bracelets, crowns and rings. There Sigurd found a magic golden helmet, the Helm of Dread, which made whoever wore it invisible. He loaded all the treasure onto his good horse Grani and rode away.

Sigurd remembered the old story the birds had spoken of. Far away, a beautiful lady lay under a spell. She slept in a castle surrounded by a wall of fire, and she would sleep forever, until a hero came who was brave enough to ride through the flames and wake her.

So Sigurd rode on through the night. On top of a hill he saw a red fire blazing up into the sky, and inside the flames stood a castle. He rode Grani straight at the fire, and Grani leaped through it as lightly as if it were heather. Inside, Sigurd found someone asleep, dressed all in armor. He lifted off the helmet, and there lay a beautiful lady.
She woke up and looked at him. "Is it Sigurd, who has broken the spell and come to wake me at last?" she asked.

Her name was Brynhild. She was a warrior maiden who rode into battle in armor. Long ago she had displeased Odin, and he had put her to sleep with a thorn from the tree of sleep. She had promised never to marry anyone who was afraid of the fire. Now Sigurd and Brynhild fell in love, and promised to be true to each other, and Sigurd gave her a ring.

The old stories tell of many more adventures after that, and the dwarf's curse on the gold did come true in the end, as such curses do. But that is a story for when you are older. For tonight, let us leave Sigurd and Brynhild on that hilltop, the dragon-slayer and the warrior maiden, with the fire burning down around them and the stars coming out overhead.
A simplified retelling of Various's “The Story of Sigurd” in The Red Fairy Book (1890). The original is listed under Other versions.
